title: Ethereum's Glamsterdam upgrade puts VASP AML controls in the spotlight
summary: The Ethereum Glamsterdam hard-fork warning about malicious block builders has direct AML implications for VASPs across APAC. Plus: what the AUSTRAC digital currency exchange penalty tells compliance teams, and one Hong Kong deadline that should already be in your calendar.
script:
JORDAN: I want to start with Ethereum, because I think compliance teams are going to file the Glamsterdam hard-fork story as a technology bulletin and miss the AML question entirely.

ALEX: I read it differently. I think the interesting signal is not the upgrade itself but the Ethereum Foundation's explicit warning about what they're calling fake or non-compliant block builders. That is the bit that should land on an MLRO's desk.

JORDAN: Right, so let's set the scene. The Ethereum Foundation has confirmed the upgrade window for Glamsterdam, which is a network-level hard fork, and simultaneously issued a developer warning that malicious or non-compliant block builders could introduce chain-halting conditions. If a bad actor can manipulate which transactions get included in a block, the downstream question for a virtual asset service provider is: can you still demonstrate that your transaction monitoring is covering the full picture of activity on-chain?

ALEX: And that is where I want to push back slightly on the framing. The chain-halt risk is real, but I think for most VASPs in this region the more immediate compliance issue is the block-builder concentration point. A handful of builders currently process the majority of Ethereum blocks. If regulators start asking whether your Know Your Transaction controls account for builder-layer manipulation, and some of them will, you need to have thought about that before the question arrives.

JORDAN: That's fair. And the honest answer for most VASPs I've spoken to is that their KYT vendors are monitoring wallet-level and transaction-level behaviour, not protocol-layer architecture. There's a gap there. It's not a crisis today, but it is the kind of gap that shows up badly in a thematic review.

ALEX: The MAS Notice 1511 for digital payment token service providers, and equivalents under the AUSTRAC AML/CTF Act for registered digital currency exchanges, both require transaction monitoring to be commensurate with the risk profile of your products. If your product runs on Ethereum, and Ethereum's block-building layer has a documented manipulation risk, that risk needs to appear somewhere in your risk assessment.

JORDAN: So the action here is specific. If you are the head of financial crime at a VASP that operates on Ethereum, pull your technology risk assessment this week and check whether protocol-layer risks are in scope for your transaction monitoring methodology. If they're not, that is a gap you want to close before your next supervisory review, not during it.

ALEX: Agreed. And flag it to your KYT vendor. They should be thinking about this too.

JORDAN: Moving on to something that lands harder and faster, because the AUSTRAC penalty against a major digital currency exchange is directly relevant to anyone running AML controls at a registered digital currency exchange in Australia or watching how AUSTRAC enforces tranche-one obligations ahead of tranche-two expansion. Forty-seven million Australian dollars, announced by AUSTRAC, for systemic failures in transaction monitoring, mule-account detection, and suspicious matter report timeliness.

ALEX: The number is significant, but I actually think the framing in the AUSTRAC announcement is the more important data point. The word "systemic" is doing a lot of work. AUSTRAC does not use that language casually. It signals that the regulator's examiners found not isolated control failures but a pattern of deficiency that ran across multiple control categories simultaneously.

JORDAN: Which is exactly the enforcement signature that the AUSTRAC website and prior penalty announcements have been moving toward over the past two years. The Westpac and CBA civil penalties in the banking sector used that same logic: individual failures matter less than whether your compliance programme has structural integrity.

ALEX: Where I'd push back is on the instinct to read this as a crypto-sector-specific story. The underlying failures here, inadequate transaction monitoring rules, poor mule-account indicators, late SMR lodgement, are the exact same findings AUSTRAC has flagged in its guidance to tranche-one reporting entities across remittance, gaming, and bullion. The sector is digital assets. The failures are not unique to it.

JORDAN: And that's the read-across for anyone who isn't a digital currency exchange. If your SMR timeliness is patchy, if your mule-account indicators haven't been reviewed since onboarding was redesigned, those are the things AUSTRAC's examiners will look for next. The penalty gives you the checklist for your own thematic review.

ALEX: So what should listeners do on this one?

JORDAN: Three things. First, if you're an AUSTRAC reporting entity of any type, pull your SMR timeliness metrics for the last six months and take them to your next risk committee. If your average time from detection to lodgement is running long, that needs remediation now. Second, review your mule-account detection rules specifically. High post-onboarding velocity, inbound from multiple unrelated retail senders, immediate outbound, those are the indicators the BNM typology bulletin on bnm.gov.my has also been flagging for digital bank mule accounts, and the pattern is consistent across jurisdictions. Third, if you are a compliance leader at a digital currency exchange in Australia, your CY 2024 annual compliance report should already have been lodged via AUSTRAC Online. If there is any doubt about whether the attestation reflects your actual control state, get independent assurance on it before the next examination cycle opens.

ALEX: Before we close, one obligation that should be live on screens in Hong Kong right now. The HKMA AML/CFT Guideline, Section 11, requires authorised institutions to submit their CY 2024 self-assessment return using the HKMA's prescribed Excel template, with Internal Audit sign-off, and the deadline is the thirtieth of September. That is eleven days away.

JORDAN: If your Internal Audit team has not yet validated the return, that conversation needs to happen before Monday. Not after.

ALEX: Exactly. The HKMA has been explicit in examination feedback that self-assessment returns submitted without genuine independent validation are treated as a governance concern in their own right, separate from whatever the substantive findings are.

JORDAN: If any of what we've covered today felt uncomfortably close to home, that is the point. The full obligation register and source links for everything we've discussed are at amlagents dot streamlit dot app. See you Monday.
